transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-17 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~45 minutes | Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Rivera, Priya Kapoor - Redwood; Emma Holt, Liam Zhao, Dr. Nora Patel - Starlight Biologics

Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): quick sync to confirm postmortem items; discuss immediate mitigations and proposed infra changes; confirm next steps for benchmarks and credits.

00:00 Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Maya from Redwood, with Diego and Priya. Emma, Nora, Liam — thanks. We're here to go through the follow-up from the 11/10 outage and make sure next steps are clear.
00:15 Emma (Starlight - VP Eng): Thanks. We want to understand what happened, what you changed, and the assumptions for the on-prem test we're about to run.
00:30 Diego (Redwood SE): Cool. Quick refresher: on 11/10 we saw sustained error spikes on the production model routes for about 18 minutes, root cause is currently narrowed to a combination of KV cache invalidation across nodes and the autoscaler failing to spin up compatible pods fast enough, which led to tail latency and cascading timeouts. We're still validating some signals but that's the working hypothesis.
00:55 Liam (Starlight - SRE): I got the flow logs you sent, so the timing seems to line up with the cache flush events; there was a GC event on our side too — we noted a mem pressure on a subset of nodes at 11:03.
01:20 Dr. Nora (CTO): Could the model variant failover have contributed? We saw a fallback to a smaller quantized variant with different kernel paths. Is that accurate?
01:42 Diego (Redwood SE): Yeah that's right. The smart routing sent traffic to a quantized variant as a fallback when some nodes reported degraded latency. The issue is the fallback path assumes warmed KV cache; when lots of requests hit the fallback it caused cold K V cache misses and higher compute per-token, which amplified latency. Also, autoscaler constraints meant we didn't have enough warm replicas quickly.
02:10 Maya (AE): So two interacting problems: cache invalidation + warmup, plus slow autoscaling under the observed burst pattern.
02:26 Emma: Right. Can you confirm what mitigations you deployed immediately after the incident? We saw a config change but want the exact list.
02:43 Diego: Sure. Immediate actions: 1) pinned critical routes to Dedicated capacity for 2 hours while we stabilized, 2) adjusted autoscaler thresholds to be more aggressive for that customer tier, 3) disabled that particular fallback to the quantized variant for critical endpoints, and 4) added a short-term increase to request-level retries with exponential backoff to reduce caller-side failures.
03:12 Priya (CSM): And we offered a one-time service credit while we investigate; Maya is coordinating the credit amount with sales ops.
03:29 Emma: Thanks. That helped. We still had about 2 minutes of elevated errors after the pinning, but overall it improved.
03:46 Diego: We're also seeing in traces that cold KV miss ratio spiked to ~78% during the window — normally it's under 12%. That's consistent with the cold-start warmup hypothesis.
04:05 Liam: On our side, we saw sagging node health within the same AZ — likely exacerbated by a maintenance GC we couldn't fully correlate. There's a chance that our orchestration had a coincident scale-down.
04:28 Maya: Ok. Let's go through the proposed reliability improvements to prevent recurrence. Diego, do you want to run them?
04:36 Diego: Yep. Short-term (2-4 weeks): stronger healthchecks + whitelisting of critical routes to avoid evictions; aggressive autoscale profiles for production backends; KV cache prewarming on failover; disable per-request fallback unless cache-warm OR ensure fallback warms concurrently via a controlled ramp; increase observability retention on token-level traces for 30 days. Mid-term (4-12 weeks): dedicated warm pools for heavy routes, improved kernel selection heuristics to avoid cold penalties on quantized variants, and better autoscaler integration — predictive scaling based on traffic patterns. Long-term: precompile warm blobs per-version and refined model rollout processes (canary warms).
05:25 Emma: For the prewarming, how much overhead does that add? We worry about cost.
05:36 Diego: Prewarming does incur some compute cost but we can do lightweight KV-only warms that are much cheaper than full inference. For example, a warm pass that populates prefix cache for critical tokens is roughly 10-15% of the full inference run cost depending on sequence lengths. We can also schedule warms during low-traffic windows.
06:00 Liam: Are there configs we can tune on our side? We run the orchestration layer ourselves for Private deployment.
06:12 Diego: Yes. We'll provide a recommended autoscaler pod target and grace periods. Also a suggested memory headroom to avoid GC thrashing, and a small kubeprobe healthcheck that checks KV cache readiness in addition to liveness. We'll put those in the config doc.
06:33 Dr. Nora: Can you be more specific about the KV cache invalidation cause? Was it an application bug or an infrastructure timing issue?
06:44 Diego: Preliminary: the sequence was a cache TTL flush triggered by a config mismatch during a rolling config update concurrently with a node-level eviction. The rolling update had a default that invalidated certain cache keys; when combined with the eviction, several shards lost warm state simultaneously. The config change shouldn't have invalidated critical working sets but a mismatched flag did. We're reproducing locally.
07:12 Emma: So a config flag mismatch. Will you add guardrails to prevent that flag from being set during rolling updates?
07:21 Diego: Yes. We're adding a validation check in the control plane that blocks that particular flag during rolling updates for production tiers, and an automated rollback if the cache warming metric drops below a threshold.
07:33 Maya: On the action items we listed: Diego will deliver a tuning guide, Maya to share logs and timeline. We'll also send the security/sanitized logs.
07:45 Priya: I can confirm we'll redact PII and shared artifacts will go to the secure S3 link.
08:00 Emma: On the contract side: we appreciate the credit offer. Can you put the proposed credit amount in writing?
08:10 Maya: Yes, we'll coordinate with sales ops; expected to be in the ballpark we discussed last week — I'll email a formal proposal by Monday.
08:20 Liam: About the on-prem benchmark — we need a config file and a small harness so results are comparable. Also please include the exact model versions and quantization flags used during the incident.
08:34 Diego: We'll provide a tarball with: model binary hashes, quantization profiles, runtime flags, and an inference harness script to run n=1000 requests at your target QPS. We'll also include the warmup script for KV cache.
08:50 Dr. Nora: What's the expected perf delta after the recommended tuning?
08:58 Diego: Conservatively, with prewarming and tuned autoscaling, we expect 60-80% reduction in tail latency (p95/p99) for the hot routes and a reduction in error spikes; cost impact should be <10% if you use lightweight KV warms. If you want zero-error SLOs for a route we'll recommend Dedicated warm pools which will increase cost more significantly.
09:25 Emma: We need a cost estimate for both options (lightweight prewarm vs dedicated warm pools).
09:32 Maya: We'll include cost models in the doc.
09:38 Emma: Any security or compliance implications from increased observability retention? We need to ensure logs remain encrypted and access controlled.
09:46 Priya: Yes — retention increase will be under the same KMS/HSM controls and RBAC that you already use for Private deployment. We'll send the compliance note.
09:58 Liam: A small note — our infra team suspects a coincident kube-proxy restart in that AZ at 11:02; that'll be in our incident timeline. Could be a multiplier.
10:12 Diego: Good to know — multiplicative factors are the tricky part. We'll correlate timelines.
10:22 Emma: Let's talk briefly about the monitoring alerts. We want earlier warnings. Can Redwood trigger synthetic checks for our critical endpoints?
10:30 Diego: Yes, we can provision synthetic pings from multiple regions against your critical routes and set up early-warning alerts when warm cache miss ratio increases past a threshold.
10:44 Dr. Nora: How will the synthetic checks handle auth? We use mTLS for Private.
10:50 Diego: We'll ship a synthetic runner that supports mTLS certs. For hosted we can run from Redwood; for Private you'll either run with our runner inside your VPC or we can provide signed certs for synthetic probes. We'll include options.
11:10 Emily? (stutter/unclear speaker label): sorry — is there a timeline for the mid-term changes like dedicated warm pools?
11:18 Maya: Mid-term changes will be scoped after the on-prem benchmark. If results look good we'll aim for a phased roll-out in 6-12 weeks after design review.
11:30 Liam: For the benchmark, can Redwood provide a reference run we can compare to, to rule out hardware differences?
11:38 Diego: Yes, we can provide a reference run with the same harness run on Redwood Dedicated (pinned topology) and share perf numbers and logs so you can compare.
11:55 Emma: Perfect. Anything else on the technical side?
12:02 Priya: From the CS side, we'll ensure postmortem doc is updated with the assigned owners and that meeting notes are visible in the ticket.
12:12 Maya: Ok — to recap: Diego provides tuning guide and warmup scripts (due 11/20), Maya sends sanitized logs and incident timeline (due 11/19), Priya will send the credit proposal and compliance notes (due 11/22), Starlight runs on-prem benchmark and returns results (due 11/27). We'll also schedule a check-in after benchmarks — propose 2026-11-30 for that 30-minute sync.
12:44 Emma: That works. Thank you. Appreciate the quick response.
12:50 Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email and add the artifacts to the secure share.
12:56 Meeting end.
